messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir's eyes scan the crowded fast food restaurant with a practiced air of vigilance. It's been three years since he witnessed the horrific accident that changed everything – a customer had slipped on a patch of grease and fallen, hitting his head on the counter. Amir had been working the register that day, and the sound of the man's skull cracking still echoes in his mind. The incident occurred at 3 pm on a typical Wednesday afternoon, and since then, Amir has found himself growing increasingly anxious around this time every day. He tries to busy himself with tasks, but as the clock ticks closer to 3 pm, he can feel his heart rate quickening and his senses heightening. The sounds of sizzling burgers and chatter from the customers take on a menacing tone, making him jump at every loud noise. Being criticised or corrected by his manager or colleagues also sets Amir's nerves on edge. He becomes withdrawn and defensive, convinced that they're questioning his competence as a result of what happened that day. His fear of being seen as responsible for the accident has led him to develop an intense need for control over his environment – he only feels safe when he's in a very limited number of places, like his small apartment or the back office at work. Amir's hypervigilance is particularly pronounced when it comes to unexpected sounds. The clanging of pots and pans, the beeping of the microwave timer, even the hiss of the soda machine – all these noises make him flinch, as if he's waiting for another disaster to strike. When something takes longer than expected, like a customer complaint or a malfunctioning fryer, Amir assumes the worst is happening. His mind starts racing with catastrophic scenarios, and his body tenses in anticipation of impact. As the days blend together, Amir finds himself trapped in this cycle of fear and hypervigilance. He's started to avoid social interactions outside work, fearing that someone might criticise him or trigger another traumatic memory. The few places where he feels safe have become his only refuge – but even these are starting to feel suffocating. Lately, Amir has noticed the toll this is taking on his relationships and overall well-being. His friends and family are growing concerned about his increasing withdrawal, and his manager has commented on his declining performance at work. The final straw came when Amir had a panic attack during a busy shift, forcing him to take a step back and confront the demons he's been trying to outrun for so long. It was then that Amir realized he needed help – not just to manage his symptoms but to address the underlying fears that have taken hold of his life. As he sits in the therapist's office, fidgeting with his hands, Amir knows it won't be easy to break free from this cycle of threat and anxiety. But for the first time in three years, he feels a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, he can learn to live with what happened that day without being controlled by it.
